summary: Version 1 passes 1 of its 4 checks, so it does not pass its own test yet. Known Mars analogs beat ordinary places: 56% of pairs (pass mark 80%). Known Mars analogs beat plain deserts: 33% of pairs (pass mark 60%). Polar and highland analogs beat ordinary places: 45% of pairs (pass mark 80%). Basalt and crater sites beat ordinary places on terrain: 84% of pairs (pass mark 80%). Most misses are small, rugged or icy analogs that fill only part of a 50 km cell, or polar sites whose cold matches but whose small day-to-night swing, low sun and clear air do not match Jezero. We publish the result as it came out; the weights and pass marks were fixed before the run. In a second run, designed after seeing those totals, each analog was checked only on the challenges it is used for: 6 of 11 checks with enough sites pass, so the second run does not pass in full either. Pooled against ordinary places (pass mark 80%): Moon 84%, Mars 60%.
not_blind_note: This is not a blind first run. A throwaway prototype scored the same test places twice on 14 November, and two lessons from it shaped this version. The weights and pass marks below were committed before this run, and the places marked blind had never been scored before.

prototype_runs.result: Moon: 67% against a pass mark of 80%
Mars: 79% against 80% (ordinary places) and 54% against 60% (plain deserts)

tests.title: Mars test
tests.plain: Known Mars analogs should beat ordinary places and plain deserts. Each place is scored on its 0.5° cell against Jezero crater, with every scored challenge weighted equally (a weighted geometric mean of the challenge scores, under the same 70% data rule as the map). A pair counts as a win when the analog scores higher; ties count half.

misses.why: Arctic: a small day-to-night swing, a low sun and clear air, far from Jezero. Polar air also reads as wet on the aridity index because so little water can evaporate. Lowest trait ranks: noon sun height 0.06, day-to-night swing (air) 0.06, dryness (aridity index) 0.12.

The valleys are smaller than a 0.5° cell, and the cell is mostly ice sheet. Polar air reads as wet on the aridity index because so little water can evaporate, and its sun is low. Lowest trait ranks: noon sun height 0.04, dust in the air 0.05, day-to-night swing (air) 0.06; 96% of the cell is permanent ice.
High Arctic: steep ground, a tiny day-to-night swing and a low sun. Lowest trait ranks: day-to-night swing (air) 0.03, noon sun height 0.03, height range 0.04.

Most of its cell is glacier, its day-to-night swing is tiny and polar air reads as wet on the aridity index. Lowest trait ranks: day-to-night swing (air) 0.01, dryness (aridity index) 0.02, noon sun height 0.03; 76% of the cell is permanent ice.
It sits in a steep Himalayan valley: almost all land on Earth is flatter. Lowest trait ranks: height range 0.02, ground under 10° 0.03, typical slope 0.03.
Its ground is rough, its sun is low and its air is clear, all far from Jezero. Lowest trait ranks: height range 0.09, ground under 10° 0.11, typical slope 0.12.
Its cell is steep valley country, and EMIT has no mineral data there. Lowest trait ranks: height range 0.01, ground under 10° 0.05, typical slope 0.05.
Its cell is steep valley country, and EMIT has no mineral data there, so the lake's salts can't count. Lowest trait ranks: height range 0.04, typical slope 0.05, ground under 10° 0.05.
A wet, rugged coast with a small day-to-night swing. Lowest trait ranks: dryness (aridity index) 0.08, typical slope 0.16, ground under 10° 0.17.
The point stands for a whole high plateau, with far more height range than Jezero's floor and clear mountain air. Lowest trait ranks: height range 0.07, dust in the air 0.12, ground under 10° 0.16.
Half of its cell is sea, and the tropical climate is warm with a small day-to-night swing. Lowest trait ranks: day-to-night swing (air) 0.01, coldest ground temperature 0.06, height range 0.07.
An Alpine gorge: steep, high-relief ground in a mostly green cell. Lowest trait ranks: height range 0.01, typical slope 0.03, ground under 10° 0.04.

Iceland's cool, wet climate has a small day-to-night swing; the lava tube itself can't be seen by any trait. Lowest trait ranks: dryness (aridity index) 0.03, day-to-night swing (air) 0.11, height range 0.14.
Its hills are far rougher than Jezero's flat crater floor, and its air is clearer than Jezero's dusty sky. Lowest trait ranks: dust in the air 0.15, height range 0.22, ground under 10° 0.24.

Not ranked: the pond sits on an Antarctic cell with no aridity value (ice sheet) and no EMIT minerals, so under 70% of the weight has data. Lowest trait ranks: height range 0.02, noon sun height 0.04, dust in the air 0.05; 86% of the cell is permanent ice.

tests.title: Moon test, part 1
tests.plain: Polar and highland analogs should beat ordinary places. It's a small group, and we say so. Each place is scored on its 0.5° cell against the Moon's south pole, with every scored challenge weighted equally (a weighted geometric mean of the challenge scores, under the same 70% data rule as the map). A pair counts as a win when the analog scores higher; ties count half.

checks.name: Polar and highland analogs beat ordinary places

misses.why: Only a small part of its cell is land; the rest is fjord and sea. Its terrain is steep and its sea climate is mild and wet, with a small yearly swing. Lowest trait ranks: typical slope 0.02, yearly temperature swing 0.02, ground under 10° 0.03; only 13% of the cell is land.

At 0.5° the rock map's main rock for its cell isn't plutonic, and the steep mountain ground scores very low on flat industrial strips. Lowest trait ranks: level ground 0.03, ground under 5° 0.05, highland-type rock 0.47.

tests.title: Moon test, part 2
tests.plain: Basalt and crater training sites stand in for the Moon's dark plains, not its pole, so they are checked only on terrain (slope, height range and ground under 10° against the south pole), with the same pass mark as the other tests. Ranking low on rock is expected, not a failure.

second_run.title: Second run: each analog on what it is used for
second_run.plain: The first run scored every known analog on its overall match, but no place on Earth copies everything, and analogs are chosen for particular jobs. This run checks each analog only on the challenges its papers say it is used for, against ordinary places on the same challenge. We designed it after seeing the first run's totals, so it helps explain the first result and is not independent proof.
second_run.summary: In a second run, designed after seeing those totals, each analog was checked only on the challenges it is used for: 6 of 11 checks with enough sites pass, so the second run does not pass in full either. Pooled against ordinary places (pass mark 80%): Moon 84%, Mars 60%.

tests.title: Moon, challenge by challenge
tests.plain: For each body and each scored challenge, the known analogs tagged for that challenge are compared with the ordinary places on that challenge's score against the default target: the result is the share of analog and ordinary pairs in which the analog scores higher, ties counting half. Mars challenges are also compared with the plain deserts. The pooled result for a body counts every analog-and-tagged-challenge entry against every ordinary place on that same challenge. A challenge with fewer than three tagged analogs is reported without a pass or fail.
